messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ethan is a 29-year-old jeweler, single, who lives and works in a quiet suburb. Three years ago, he returned from a six-month deployment as a relief worker in a conflict zone in the Middle East. His most vivid memory is of a market square where he had been distributing supplies. A mortar round struck a nearby stall, and in the chaos that followed, he found himself pinned beneath debris, the air filled with the screams of children and the smell of burning metal. He had been sure he was going to die. For weeks afterward, he could not stop replaying the sound of those screams.

Now, back in his workshop, Ethan’s life has narrowed. The sound of a child crying in the street outside his store—a trigger he cannot predict or control—can instantly drop him back into that market square, the memory arriving with a visceral, disorienting clarity. The memory feels more real than the present, more vivid than any ordinary recollection of his day. In response, he has developed a set of strategies to manage these intrusions. He forces himself to think only positive thoughts, repeating phrases like "I am safe now" until his jaw aches. He also reminds himself that it could have been worse, that he survived, that others did not. But these efforts often backfire: pushing the image away only makes it return with greater force, and the act of comparing his trauma to a worse, imagined fate somehow makes the memory feel even more present and menacing.

The memory itself has become a trigger. The sheer intensity of the emotional flashback—the terror without a clear image—can set his heart racing, and that pounding in his chest, in turn, feels like a new threat, one that pulls him back to the memory of his heart hammering against the rubble. This cycle has made him hypervigilant. He now scans every environment for potential weapons or dangerous objects, a habit that is exhausting in his own shop, where tools and heavy equipment are everywhere. He feels unsafe unless his back is against a wall, a posture he has adopted at his workbench, which his colleagues have begun to notice. Even when his boss or his mother tells him he is safe, he finds it impossible to believe. This pervasive sense of threat primes him for a reaction: a colleague touching his shoulder unexpectedly sends a jolt of pure adrenaline through him, instantly triggering the full memory of being pinned and helpless. The scanning itself also triggers the memory, as his eyes catch on a pair of shears or a heavy mallet, and his mind supplies a flash of shrapnel or a gun barrel.

The downward comparisons and forced positive thinking are meant to reduce his distress, but they have instead cemented a new, painful logic: the only way to control the memory is to never be caught off guard. This means he is always watching, always bracing, and the constant vigilance has worn him down. He has stopped going out to dinner with friends because restaurants are too unpredictable—a child’s laugh, a hand on his shoulder. His relationship with his family has become strained; they see him as distant and jumpy, and he cannot explain why he flinches when his sister hugs him. What finally brought him to therapy was a moment last week when a customer’s toddler began to cry. Ethan felt the full emotional force of the explosion hit him without any visual memory—just pure, disembodied terror—and he had to excuse himself to the back room, shaking. He is terrified that his mind is breaking, that the memories are becoming more real than his actual life. More than anything, he is hoping to learn how to stop the cycle, to find a way to feel safe in his own skin again.
